title: Site authorisation and sanitation task boundaries
audience: Cleaners and contractors visiting food-processing sites to carry out sanitation tasks.
learningOutcomes: Identify the operator-approved sanitation procedure and the person who authorises work before any task starts.
Mark restricted spaces, unknown hazards and off-limits equipment on a site plan.
Stop the planned work when production release or task ownership is unclear, and record a hold rather than an unapproved workaround.

instruction.heading: The site owns the sanitation programme
instruction.body: On a food-processing site, the facility's food safety team owns the sanitation programme, not the visiting cleaner. Before any sanitation work, you need three things in writing: the operator-approved sanitation procedure, confirmation of the production shutdown, and the name of the food safety or production supervisor who authorises the work. Explain who can grant access, who reviews deviations, and who can authorise restart of production. If any of these is missing, the work does not start.

instruction.heading: Observe without disturbing production
instruction.body: Review the signed production release, and identify which manager owns access and sanitising clearance. On the site plan, mark every restricted space and every unknown hazard before you propose any activity. Treat machinery, ingredients and processing surfaces as off-limits until they are specifically authorised for the work. A cleaner who moves a product or touches a line to see what is there has already changed the situation.

instruction.heading: Stopping on unclear ownership
instruction.body: When the production line has not been released, or when it is not clear who owns the task, stop. Do not look for a workaround. Escalate to the responsible authorised person, protect the zone, and document the hold and the referral. Do not claim that the area is sanitised or released, because that decision belongs to the facility.

instruction.heading: Recording the hold
instruction.body: Record the date, the zone, the issue, the source of the authorisation, the action that was withheld, the person notified and the decision that is still pending. The record must never describe validated sanitation, allergen freedom or microbiological clearance, unless an authorised person has issued that result.

procedure: Confirm the operator-approved sanitation procedure, the production shutdown and the authorising supervisor in writing.
Review the signed production release and identify the access and sanitising owner.
Mark restricted spaces, unknown hazards and off-limits equipment on the site plan.
Stop and escalate where production release or task ownership is unclear.
Record the hold, the referral and the pending decision, with no clearance claim.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is asked to start sanitising a line before the production release is signed.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not start. The production release is not signed, so the line is not authorised for work. Escalate to the authorised supervisor, protect the zone, and record the hold and the pending decision without claiming any clearance.

equipmentAndPpe: Site-issued PPE as the site instruction requires.
Site plan for marking restricted areas.

commonErrors.error: Starting sanitation on a line that has not been released.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the signed release and the authorising person before any work.

commonErrors.error: Inferring a dose or contact time from a similar site.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the operator-issued current instruction.

commonErrors.error: Recording the area as sanitised after a visual check.
commonErrors.prevention: Record only what was done, and leave clearance to the facility.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A food safety program under Standard 3.2.1 is needed only for food businesses that the enforcing agency has placed in a priority category; the FSANZ guide to that standard has a first edition dated June 2007. This lesson does not confer any food safety clearance or qualification.
Site access and task authority on a food-processing site are set by the operator. This lesson does not grant any site authority, sanitation clearance or qualification.

Safety details for every chemical, hazardous or not, need to reach all people on site, and they sit on the label and the SDS. The register has to cover hazardous chemicals that are used, handled or kept on site, each entry needs an up-to-date SDS attached, and the register must be easy for workers to reach (Safe Work Australia, no date shown). Check your state or territory regulator for extra rules.

qualityStandard: Authority and task owner identified from a fictional authorisation sheet.
Restricted spaces and off-limits equipment marked on the simulated site plan.
Hold and referral recorded without a clearance claim.
documentationEvidence: Hold and referral record with the pending decision.
summary: The facility owns the sanitation programme; confirm authority in writing first.
Mark restricted and off-limits areas before any activity.
Stop and escalate on unclear release or ownership.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must be confirmed before sanitation starts on a food-processing line?
options: That the cleaner has a spare cloth and a spare pair of gloves ready
That the line looks clean from the walkway at the start of the shift
The operator-approved procedure, the shutdown and the authorising supervisor

knowledgeChecks.question: Production has not been released and task ownership is unclear. What do you do?
options: Stop, protect the zone, and escalate with a recorded hold
Find a workaround to keep the schedule on track for the week
Start on the non-critical side while the question is sorted out

knowledgeChecks.question: Can a cleaner record a line as sanitised after a visual check?
options: Yes, appearance is enough when the line looks clean and dry at the time
No, clearance is decided by the facility, and the record must not claim it
Yes, if the supervisor is not present to check the line at the time of the clean

knowledgeChecks.question: What must be marked on the site plan before any activity is proposed?
options: Every restricted space and every unknown hazard
